narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 93.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, compared to an average around the middle of the class among accepted students, signaled consistent academic struggle in law school. This was the dominant reason the model saw high risk.

Your LSAT score of 31 was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. It sits noticeably below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, further increasing the estimated chance you would not pass the bar.

Other details such as your high family income, 2.7 undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not outweigh the top three signals.

You should focus on strengthening the areas that hurt your profile most. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or spending time on rigorous academic preparation and practice exams that mirror the bar to demonstrate you can overcome past ranking challenges. With clearer evidence of improvement in these key areas, future applications may receive a different outcome. (218 words)
